newsitem.title: UK: Dlr eyes US data in Europe, stg recoups some loss.
newsitem.headline: Dlr eyes US data in Europe, stg recoups some loss.

text.p: The dollar drifted against the mark and yen at Europe's midday as operators backed away from it ahead of U.S. payrolls data due later today and focused on sterling in the aftermath of Britain's parliamentary elections.

The pound had spiralled down against the mark and dollar in early Europe as profit-taking set in. Sterling rose overnight while the Labour party stormed to a landslide victory and took power for the first time in 18 years.
A Labour win had been fully anticipated, but the size of the party's majority -- expected to be about 180 in a 659-seat parliament -- caught many by surprise.

"Although things have cooled down a bit, there was selling in sterling because people were afraid that with Labour free to do as it likes in government, there was some question as to whether it will do what investors are hoping for," said one senior dealer at a Japanese bank in London.
"Until we see some policy announcements and the cabinet line-up, there's going to be nervousness over sterling."

The pound had climbed off its lows by midday, and was at $1.6090/00 and 2.7790/00 marks at 1100 GMT, still down from the highs hit overnight at $1.6280 and 2.8035. It was at $1.6236/42 and 2.7935/45 late on Thursday ahead of the poll results.

"The sheer size of the (Labour) victory has taken some of the shine off the pound already and that could continue...but although it's coming off a bit, it's still going to remain pretty firm in the near term," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International here.
"Once the new Chancellor (finance minister) convinces the markets that his policies are not going to be radical, sterling should pick up a bit," Lyons said.
The dollar, which was drifting with a strong bias, was unfazed by the election results, which traders said was as expected.
The dollar was at 1.7253/58 marks and 126.65/75 yen against 1.7198/03 and 126.60/65 in late European trade on Thursday.
The currency market's attention should return to the dollar when U.S. April payrolls data are announced at 1230 GMT, analysts said.

The market has seen a glut of key U.S. data this week, with some showing conflicting signals. The April NAPM yesterday showed a drop in indices on business activity and prices, while Wednesday's GDP growth was far above expectations. And employment costs dropped according to data released on Tuesday.

"We're in a situation in which interest rate expectations and bond yields have begun to move against the dollar. The dollar has been supported so far by inflows into the bond and equities markets, but the pattern tends to be of short-term predominance," said Chris Turner, currency strategist at BZW.
"Eventually the dollar will come down in line with interest rate expectations. Another weak number today in the non-farm payrolls could see the dollar move down," Turner said.
The headline April payrolls figure is forecast to rise by 211,000 after increasing 175,000 in March, and the unemployment rate is expected to be unchanged at 5.2 percent.

"The market's already seen very strong GDP figures, so jobs figures that are a bit better than expected aren't going to make much difference to sentiment at this stage," the Japanese bank trader said.

Elsewhere the Irish pound, which had in the past two days dropped heavily against the mark and sterling, managed to climb higher. The punt was helped by a surprise 50-basis-point rise in Ireland's short-term facility rate to 6.75 percent late on Thursday, and by sterling's drop in the wake of the British election.
